c.v: This stage gives the bench its third scenario: a mission cancelled while it is running. The route the follower drives stops being a set of parameters read at startup and becomes an action goal, so something outside the node can ask for a route, watch how far along it is, and take it back.
The decision worth defending is writing our own action rather than bending one that exists.

ships a single action, Fibonacci, whose goal is one integer, and forcing a route through it would cost every later reader an explanation. A package of our own costs a fourth package, a build-order dependency, and generated code that every consumer rebuilds when the file changes. What it buys is a goal that carries the route, feedback that says how far along the robot is, and a result that says how far it got, all visible from

What we can now show: the scenario cancels the mission partway through, the robot comes to rest within 1.5 seconds and stays where it stopped, no further goal is reached, and the run leaves no process behind. A follower that never checks
fails three of those five lines.

prints the three parts of it.

Cancellation is the first thing the bench asks for that a topic cannot carry. A topic is fire and forget: the follower reads its goals from parameters at startup, and nothing can ask it to stop that is not a stop command aimed at the robot. What this scenario needs is a request with an identity, so that it can be taken back, and progress that belongs to that request rather than to the node. That is what an action is, and the topic on services and actions built one end to end.
The interface is the part with a real cost, so decide it deliberately.

order. You could send a route through it by agreeing that the order means something else, and every person who read the code afterwards would need that agreement explained. The alternative is a package of your own, and here is the bill.
It costs a fourth package in the workspace, which colcon has to build before
because the generated headers come out of it. It costs generated code in three languages whether or not you want them. It costs a rebuild of every consumer each time the

file changes, which is the reason interface packages are kept small and separate rather than living inside the node package. And once anything outside your repository uses it, a change to a field is a change to an interface that somebody else has compiled against.

It buys a goal that says what it is, feedback that arrives while the work runs, a result that says what was achieved, and a cancel path with rules the client library already implements. It also buys the command line:
work on it with no code from you, which is worth more during a failed scenario than it sounds now.

items.v: . The three parts are separated by
, in the order goal, result, feedback:

blocks.text:
# Goal: the route to drive, in the odometry frame.
float64[] goals_x
float64[] goals_y
float64 tolerance_m
---
# Result: how far the robot got, whatever ended the goal.
int32 goals_reached
---
# Feedback: where it is now, one message per odometry message.
int32 goals_reached
float64 range_to_goal_m

c.v: The result carries one number on purpose. Whether the goal succeeded, was cancelled or was aborted is already in the action's own status, which the client gets with the result, so a
field beside it would be a second copy of a fact that can now disagree with the first. Put in a result what the status cannot say, and nothing else.
The two parallel arrays are the same shape the route parameters had, and for the same reason: an interface field can hold a list of numbers but not a list of pairs.
already refuses a mismatched pair, so the server has the check it needs and the failure is a rejected goal rather than a short route.

The pattern is the one the services and actions topic built: the work runs on a callback of the node rather than on a thread of its own, the goal handle is kept in a member because the action server holds only a weak pointer to it, and

is checked on every tick of that work. The follower already has the right heartbeat for it. It does its work in the odometry callback, one command per message, so the cancel is checked once per odometry message and the answer comes back within one period.

Cancellation and a lost input ask the robot for the same thing, so three of the five checks are the missing-odometry ones with the cue renamed. The two that are new are what makes cancellation different: the robot must not carry on afterwards, and no goal may be reached after the request.

c.v: The fourth check is the one that does the work. It measures from the cancel to the end of the run rather than to the moment the robot first came to rest, so a follower that stops politely and then carries on, which is what a cancel handled in the wrong place looks like, produces the same 0.54 m as one that never stopped at all. The fifth is the requirement a person would state first and a test would leave out: a cancelled mission does not get to finish.

Add tests for both verdicts, one for a cancel that never went out, and one for a robot already standing still when the cancel arrived, which must fail on the second check rather than pass on the third.
